- If sentiment is consistently high (≥0.7) over recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast slightly, especially after sharp spikes.
- If sentiment is low (≤0.3) and price is trending down, model often underestimates; adjust upward to reflect mean reversion or support.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior day), model frequently overshoots; cap forecast at 1–2% below peak or use lagged sentiment to dampen momentum.
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating high/low), model exhibits erratic behavior; smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 days or using sentiment-weighted median.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days of decline after peak), model often fails to correct; apply downward bias of 1–3% for 3–5 day horizon.
- For 30-day forecasts, if history shows strong downward trend + low sentiment, model often ignores trend; add 1–2% downward adjustment to reflect sentiment-driven bearish bias.
- If sentiment is rising (increasing over 3–5 days) and price is falling, model may misread sentiment; forecast should reflect sentiment reversal or pause in decline.
